title: DP-BREM: Differentially-Private and Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning with Client Momentum

C-a.quote: Since DP-BREM assumes a trusted server (who can obtain clients' local models or updates), we further develop the final solution called DP-BREM+ , which achieves the same DP and robustness properties as DP-BREM without a trusted server by utilizing secure aggregation techniques, where DP noise is securely and jointly generated by the clients.
C-a.locator: Abstract; the purpose of each non-robustness component is stated by the paper itself -- "Recall that R is for DP, while C is for robustness" (§5.3), "In our initial solution DP-BREM, DP is achieved by adding noise to the aggregated momentum, and we account for the privacy cost from the momentum" (§1), and of the secure-aggregation layer, "which protects the information of private inputs after the noisy aggregate is released" (§6)

C-b.quote: Taken together, our solution achieves a better privacy-utility tradeoff and Byzantine robustness over five baseline protocols.
C-b.locator: §7 Conclusion; the paired properties are privacy and robustness, not two defenses

C-c.quote: Experimental results show that DP-BREM outperforms both approaches.
C-c.locator: §3.2; the metric is the composed system's own end-to-end utility under attack, "We evaluate the testing accuracy of the global model within T iterations" (§6.1), reported per attack (IPM, ALIE, MTB, sign-flipping) in Figures 4-5 and Tables 3-5

C-d.quote: Impact of R in DP-BREM/+ . Figure 5 shows how the accuracy changes w.r.t. the record-level clipping bound R in DP-BREM/+ . The results demonstrate that when there are fewer Byzantine clients (i.e., smaller δB ) or the noise multiplier σ is smaller (i.e., larger ε), we need to set a larger R to obtain better accuracy.
C-d.locator: §6.2, Figure 5; R is the DP stage's parameter ("Recall that R is for DP, while C is for robustness", §5.3), swept with the robust momentum estimator, the client-level clipping bound C and the attack all held fixed

C-e.quote: Limitation 2: large impact on Byzantine robustness. Since the DP noise is added locally to each client's gradient before momentum-based clipping, it leads to a negative impact on Byzantine robustness: the noisy client momentum mt,i has larger variance than the noise-free one, which leads to larger bias and variance on the clipping step ClipC (mt,i − mt−1 ). Furthermore, this impact will be enlarged when there [are more Byzantine clients]
C-e.locator: §3.2, Limitation 2 of DP-LFH; the composed-system consequence is stated at §5.3, "due to the format of |B|/n + sqrt(d) sigma / (n q), the impact from DP noise is independent of the increase of Byzantine clients |B| (versus Limitation 2 of DP-LFH in Section 3.2)"

coder_note:
C-a = NO UNDER AMENDMENT 3, AND THE PAPER'S OWN SENTENCE DOES THE WORK: "Recall that R is for DP, while C is for robustness." Exactly one component here has resisting malicious updates as its stated purpose -- the momentum-based clipping of the BREM estimator. The Gaussian noise is there for differential privacy, and the secure-aggregation layer of DP-BREM+ is there so the same privacy holds without a trusted server. This is the same shape as SHARE and zPROBE and is coded the same way.

THE BORDERLINE, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN, AND IT IS CLOSER HERE THAN IN ANY PRIOR ROW. A reader could code C-a = YES on the pair (client momentum, clipping): both are inside BREM, both are applied to the same round in sequence, and the paper states a ROBUSTNESS purpose for each -- "LFH achieves robustness via client momentum with the motivation of averaging the updates of each client over time, thus reducing the variance of the honest clients and exposing the small malicious perturbations of Byzantine clients that are undetectable in a single round but accumulate over time" (§3.1), while the clipping bounds each client's deviation. Under Amendment 3's purpose test both legs pass, so the question is only whether they are TWO mechanisms or one published aggregation rule. It is coded as one, for the reason the paper gives: it treats LFH's robust aggregator as a unit inherited from prior work and locates its own contribution elsewhere -- "aggregating a subset It of clients in (12) is one of the major differences from LFH" (§4.1) -- and it never enumerates momentum and clipping as two features of its own the way FLTrust enumerates its three. Coding it YES would raise our DESIGN rate; coding it NO is the conservative direction, and it keeps this row consistent with SHARE (robust oracle as a black box) and BROADCAST. The primary code is NO either way, because C-d = YES.

C-e IS THE STRONGEST ATTRIBUTION QUOTATION IN THE FRAME SO FAR, AND IT IS OUR OWN ATTENUATION CHANNEL WRITTEN OUT FOR DP NOISE. Limitation 2 says the upstream stage's noise inflates the variance of what the downstream stage sees, and therefore inflates the bias and variance of the downstream clipping step -- an upstream operation degrading a downstream defense's ability to separate malicious from honest, argued analytically and then repaired by moving the noise downstream of the aggregation. §5.3 completes it by showing the repaired composition's error term no longer couples to |B|.

THE ANALYTIC ROUTE IS ALSO PRESENT, AND c_d_route RECORDS THE EMPIRICAL ONE. Limitation 2 varies the DP noise's position and presence against a fixed robust estimator in the bound, which is BROADCAST's analytic route to C-d. Figure 5's sweep of R is the same contrast run as an experiment, so the route field takes the stricter, empirical form and this note records that both are present. Tables 4 and 5 add two more sweeps (client-level clipping bound C, sampling rate q), but C is the downstream mechanism's own parameter and q changes who is aggregated, so neither is the basis for the code.
